opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. I think the core insight is that we've been doing computation in a way that fights physics rather than working with it. If you look at how we run AI today, especially probabilistic AI, we take deterministic digital hardware, these transistors that we've engineered to be as noise-free as possible, and then we spend enormous amounts of energy simulating randomness on top of them. We generate pseudo-random numbers, we run Monte Carlo sampling, we do all this work to emulate stochasticity that nature gives you for free.

Thermodynamic computing flips that around. The idea is that physical systems naturally fluctuate. They're constantly sampling from distributions because of thermal noise. So instead of suppressing that noise at great energetic cost and then re-simulating it in software, you can harness it directly. You design hardware whose natural physical dynamics, its equilibration toward a steady state, correspond to the computation you want: sampling from a probability distribution, doing inference, even certain kinds of linear algebra.

When you think about the energy requirements of intelligence through that lens, you realize a lot of the cost is overhead from the mismatch between the algorithm and the substrate. Intelligence, at some level, is about modeling uncertainty, compressing the world into a generative model and sampling from it. That's fundamentally a thermodynamic process. Biology figured this out; your brain runs on something like twenty watts, and it's a noisy, stochastic, analog system. It's not fighting its own noise, it's exploiting it.

So my view is that if we want to scale intelligence, and I do think we should want to scale it massively, we can't just keep building bigger data centers of deterministic chips and hope the energy works out. We need to go down the stack and rethink the physics of computation itself. There are potentially orders of magnitude of efficiency gains available by matching the hardware to the native thermodynamics of the problem.

And more broadly, I think this connects to a bigger picture: life and intelligence are processes that emerge because they're good at capturing free energy and dissipating it as heat. Building computers that operate in harmony with that principle rather than against it feels like the natural next step. It's less about squeezing a few more percent out of existing GPUs and more about aligning our technology with the way the universe actually computes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to understand is that the energy cost of intelligence isn't really a fixed property of intelligence itself. It's a property of the substrate we've chosen to run it on. Right now we run neural networks on digital hardware, and digital hardware is this incredible feat of engineering where we take a physical system that's inherently noisy and analog and we spend enormous amounts of energy forcing it to be deterministic. Every bit flip is a battle against thermodynamics. You're pumping entropy out of the system constantly to keep those ones and zeros crisp. And then, ironically, we take that pristine deterministic machine and we use it to sample from probability distributions. We generate pseudorandom numbers, we do Monte Carlo, we run diffusion models, we add noise back in. So we're paying twice. We pay to suppress the noise and then we pay again to simulate it.

Thermodynamic computing is basically saying, stop fighting physics and start collaborating with it. Nature already computes probabilistically for free. Every physical system at finite temperature is constantly sampling from a Boltzmann distribution. That's just what matter does. So if you can build hardware where the physics of the device is the computation, where the equilibrium state of your circuit is the posterior you wanted to sample, then the energy cost drops not by a constant factor but by orders of magnitude, because you're no longer paying the overhead of pretending to be a Turing machine.

And I think this reframes the whole question. The conventional narrative is that intelligence requires exponentially growing compute and therefore exponentially growing energy, and we're going to need nuclear plants next to every data center. And maybe some of that is true in the near term. But the deeper point is that the brain runs at roughly twenty watts, and it does it precisely because it's a noisy, stochastic, thermodynamic system that evolution tuned to exploit those fluctuations rather than suppress them. So the lesson isn't that intelligence is intrinsically expensive. The lesson is that we're currently running it in the most expensive possible way.

Where I think this gets really interesting philosophically is that it suggests intelligence is in some sense a thermodynamic phenomenon already. Learning is a process of lowering free energy, of finding structure in data so you can represent it more compactly. Inference is sampling from a conditioned distribution. These are not metaphors, they're literally the same mathematics as statistical mechanics. So building computers that are natively thermodynamic isn't a hack or a specialized accelerator. It's arguably closing a loop and putting intelligence back on the kind of physical substrate it was always implicitly describing.

astra-6.text:
I think it changes the question from “How much energy do we need to power intelligence?” to “How effectively can we use physical processes to perform intelligent computation?” Intelligence is implemented in matter, so ultimately it has to obey thermodynamics. But that doesn’t mean the energy cost of today’s hardware is some fundamental cost of intelligence.

In conventional computing, we spend a lot of effort making devices behave deterministically, suppressing thermal fluctuations, and moving information between memory and processors. That’s enormously useful, but for a lot of machine learning, what we actually want is sampling, inference, or finding good configurations in a very large space. So you can ask: could the fluctuations themselves become part of the computation? Could we engineer a physical system whose natural dynamics do something useful for us?

That’s the promise of thermodynamic computing. You’re still paying an energy cost to prepare the system, control it, and read out the result. There’s no free lunch. And you have to compare the whole system against conventional hardware at a useful level of accuracy and speed.

But it opens up a different design philosophy: develop the algorithm and the physics together. Instead of treating energy as just the electricity bill at the end, treat it as a central part of how the computation works.

r001.rationale: The response discusses energy-efficient computation and says current hardware costs are not fundamental, but it does not cite human intelligence’s low energy use or connect that to challenging power-generation needs for scaling intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes the question from “How much energy does intelligence require?” to “How much energy does our particular implementation of intelligence require?” Those are very different questions.

In conventional computing, we spend a lot of energy making the hardware behave deterministically, suppressing fluctuations, and then, for probabilistic algorithms, we generate randomness again. With thermodynamic computing, the idea is to use those physical fluctuations as part of the computation. You engineer a system whose natural dynamics perform some of the sampling or inference you want.

That doesn’t mean intelligence becomes free. You still have to account for preparing the system, controlling it, reading it out, and how quickly and accurately it produces an answer. But it suggests that we should design the algorithm and the physics together. The energy cost of today’s hardware isn’t necessarily a fundamental energy cost of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses implementation-dependent energy costs but does not invoke the low energy use of human intelligence or challenge the need for massive increases in power generation.
